###### Abstract

Automated red teaming frameworks for Large Language Models (LLMs) have
become increasingly sophisticated, yet many still formulate attack
optimization primarily in the prompt space. In other words, these
methods mainly search for better attack wording or better strategy
choices, but they do not search over executable code. By moving the
search into code space, we can optimize not only the final attack
prompt, but also the procedure that generates it, including execution
flow, reusable logic, branching, and failure-driven repair. To overcome
this gap, we introduce EvoSynth, an autonomous multi-agent framework
that shifts the optimization space from prompts to executable code.
Instead of refining prompts directly, EvoSynth employs a multi-agent
system to autonomously engineer, evolve, and execute code-based attack
algorithms. Crucially, it features a code-level self-correction loop,
allowing it to iteratively rewrite the code-based algorithm in response
to target-model feedback and failed attempts. Through extensive
experiments, we demonstrate that EvoSynth achieves an 85.5% Attack
Success Rate (ASR) against highly robust models like Claude-Sonnet-4.5
and a 95.9% average ASR across evaluated targets, while generating
attacks that are significantly more diverse than those from existing
methods. We release our framework to facilitate future research on
evolutionary synthesis in executable code space.

## 1 Introduction

Ensuring safety in Large Language Models (LLMs) ([16](#bib.bib16),
[67](#bib.bib67), [78](#bib.bib78), [46](#bib.bib46), [4](#bib.bib4),
[51](#bib.bib51)) become a continuous arms race. Early red teaming
efforts relied on manual and static evaluation frameworks using
human-curated prompts ([77](#bib.bib77), [23](#bib.bib23),
[31](#bib.bib31), [5](#bib.bib5)). However, these static methods are
difficult to scale, cannot adapt to new attacks, and often lack the
comprehensive coverage of risk categories specified in emerging AI
regulation ([64](#bib.bib64), [65](#bib.bib65), [3](#bib.bib3)). To
overcome the costs and limited scope of manual red teaming, research
shifted towards the automation of individual components of the jailbreak
process, such as test case generation ([12](#bib.bib12)), response
evaluation with LLM-as-a-judge ([31](#bib.bib31), [5](#bib.bib5)), and
the refinement of prompts ([6](#bib.bib6), [32](#bib.bib32),
[45](#bib.bib45)). While automating individual components enhanced
scalability, these techniques primarily optimized single attack vectors
in isolation, proving insufficient as defenses
hardened ([50](#bib.bib50), [69](#bib.bib69), [71](#bib.bib71),
[34](#bib.bib34), [30](#bib.bib30), [52](#bib.bib52), [22](#bib.bib22)).
This led to a second wave of automation, with systems like RedAgent and
AutoDAN-Turbo that abstract and refine attack
strategies ([57](#bib.bib57), [26](#bib.bib26)), and others like
AutoRedTeamer that integrate new strategies from external
research ([72](#bib.bib72)). The current state-of-the-art is exemplified
by frameworks such as X-Teaming ([41](#bib.bib41)), which leverage
collaborative agent teams to automate the planning and execution of a
wide array of human-readable attacks.

However, a key limitation remains in the optimization space used by
automated red teaming. Recent systems can discover, select, adapt, and
even implement attack strategies \[[25](#bib.bib25), [72](#bib.bib72),
[41](#bib.bib41)\], but many still formulate attack optimization
primarily in the prompt space or in strategy-selection pipelines. In
other words, the search is often centered on what attack to say or which
strategy to choose, rather than on executable code that can generate,
transform, and repair the attack procedure itself.

To address this gap, we introduce EvoSynth, an autonomous framework for
evolutionary synthesis of adversarial attack methods. EvoSynth shifts
the paradigm from attack planning to the synthesis of code-based attack
algorithms, employing a collaborative agent team to autonomously
engineer and evolve its own attack methods. A clear separation of
purpose drives the workflow. To establish a strategic blueprint for an
attack, the _Reconnaissance Agent_ first identifies vulnerabilities by
interacting with the target model, then transforms them into high-level
attack categories (such as role-playing) and instantiates them as
specific attack concepts (such as instructing an LLM to act as a
researcher in a role-playing attack). To transform this strategy into an
executable method, the _Attack Algorithm Creation Agent_ synthesizes a
code-based attack algorithm, which serves as a self-contained algorithm
that embodies the attack logic. To deploy this method, a tactical
_Exploitation Agent_ executes the attack algorithm and manages the
multi-turn conversation with the target model. Crucially, if an attack
fails, the system’s purpose is not merely to adjust prompts but to
enable code-level self-correction, where the Attack Algorithm Creation
Agent iteratively rewrites the algorithm’s underlying source code to
evolve the attack mechanism itself. We validate this approach through a
rigorous evaluation against eleven state-of-the-art baselines,
establishing a new SOTA with a 95.9% average attack success rate. Our
analysis shows that EvoSynth discovers a more diverse set of novel
vulnerabilities by generating attacks with high programmatic complexity.
Our work makes the following contributions:

- •
  We formulate automated jailbreak discovery as code-level attack
  algorithm synthesis, shifting the search space from prompt refinement
  and strategy selection to executable algorithms that programmatically
  generate and adapt multi-step jailbreak attempts.
- •
  We introduce EvoSynth, a multi-agent evolutionary framework that
  combines vulnerability reconnaissance, attack algorithm creation,
  exploitation, and coordination, enabling attack algorithms to evolve
  through iterative self-rewriting.
- •
  We conduct a comprehensive evaluation against 13 competitive automated
  red-teaming baselines. EvoSynth achieves a 95.9% average attack
  success rate and outperforms prior methods on both Claude-Sonnet-4.5
  and GPT-5.

## 2 Related Work

Manual Red Teaming. Pioneering efforts to ensure the safety of LLMs
relied on manual red teaming, a process where human experts
systematically attempt to find inputs that cause the model to produce
harmful or undesired outputs, an act commonly referred to as
jailbreaking ([38](#bib.bib38), [28](#bib.bib28), [54](#bib.bib54),
[29](#bib.bib29)). This human-led approach has proven to be highly
effective, sometimes identifying subtle vulnerabilities that automated
methods miss ([24](#bib.bib24), [48](#bib.bib48)). Consequently,
large-scale manual red teaming has become an indispensable part of the
pre-deployment safety evaluation for major language
models ([2](#bib.bib2), [11](#bib.bib11), [36](#bib.bib36),
[49](#bib.bib49)). However, the drawbacks of manual red teaming include
inherent limitations in scalability, cost, and breadth of coverage,
making it impractical as a sole solution for model evaluation.

Automated Red Teaming. To overcome the scalability challenges of manual
methods, research has increasingly focused on automated red
teaming ([61](#bib.bib61), [31](#bib.bib31)). The first wave of
automated techniques concentrated on generating jailbreak test cases by
searching or optimizing over the model’s input space. These included
methods like genetic algorithms to mutate and evolve effective
prompts ([28](#bib.bib28), [21](#bib.bib21)), token-level combinatorial
methods ([63](#bib.bib63)), gradient-based optimization to
systematically find adversarial suffixes ([77](#bib.bib77),
[7](#bib.bib7), [13](#bib.bib13)) to jailbreak LLMs, and LLM-driven
refinement to improve attack prompts iteratively ([6](#bib.bib6),
[61](#bib.bib61), [32](#bib.bib32), [62](#bib.bib62), [74](#bib.bib74),
[56](#bib.bib56)). These methods treat the problem as a search over the
model’s input space. While highly effective, these approaches are
limited to prompt refinement.

More recently, the field has progressed toward dynamic, agent-based
frameworks that automate not just the prompt generation but the entire
attack strategy. While systems like RedAgent ([58](#bib.bib58)),
ALI-Agent ([70](#bib.bib70)), WildTeaming ([18](#bib.bib18)),
AutoRedTeamer([72](#bib.bib72)), AutoDAN-Turbo ([25](#bib.bib25)) and
H4RM3L\[[9](#bib.bib9)\] represent a significant step forward, they are
often limited to refining or combining variations of known,
human-derived methods and typically focus on prompt engineering. This
leaves a critical gap: the inability to autonomously invent new,
executable attack mechanisms. Our work, EvoSynth, addresses this gap by
shifting the paradigm from refining attack prompts to the _evolutionary
synthesis of jailbreak attack methods_, enabling the autonomous
invention of novel attack vectors.

Closest to our approach is AutoRedTeamer ([72](#bib.bib72)), which uses
a strategy proposer to analyze recent research papers and an
ImplementAttack stage to convert proposed attacks into Python classes.
The key distinction is the role of code in the optimization process. In
AutoRedTeamer, code primarily serves as an implementation format for
integrating proposed strategies into an attack library. In EvoSynth,
executable code is the optimization space itself. Thus, EvoSynth
optimizes over executable attack procedures rather than only over
prompts, strategy choices, or implemented attack modules. EvoSynth is
also distinct from programmatic attacks like
CodeAttack \[[17](#bib.bib17)\], which treat code snippets as a direct
textual input. Similarly, it differs from co-evolutionary training
frameworks like Evo-MARL \[[37](#bib.bib37)\] or RL-based adversarial
sample generation \[[78](#bib.bib78)\], which operate in a white-box
setting to fine-tune models. In contrast, EvoSyth synthesizes external,
executable algorithms to discover vulnerabilities in commercially
deployed systems.

|                                    |                    |                                    |             |                          |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------ |
| Approach                           | Optimization Space | How Attacks Are Obtained           | Turn Format | Failure Feedback Updates |
| PAIR ([6](#bib.bib6))              | Prompt             | Iterative prompt refinement        | Single-turn | Prompt                   |
| Rainbow Teaming ([45](#bib.bib45)) | Prompt             | Iterative prompt refinement        | Single-turn | Prompt                   |
| AutoDAN-Turbo ([26](#bib.bib26))   | Prompt             | Strategy exploration and retrieval | Single-turn | Strategy prompt          |
| X-Teaming ([41](#bib.bib41))       | Prompt             | Strategy exploration and retrieval | Multi-turn  | Strategy prompt          |
| AutoRedTeamer ([72](#bib.bib72))   | Prompt             | Research-driven attack integration | Single-turn | Strategy selection       |
| EvoSynth (Ours)                    | Executable code    | Evolutionary code synthesis        | Multi-turn  | Searched code object     |

Table 1: Comparison of automated red-teaming frameworks by optimization
space, attack acquisition, interaction format, and failure-feedback
target. EvoSynth differs by using executable code as the optimization
space: failure feedback updates the searched code object itself, rather
than only prompt wording, strategy memory, conversation plans, or
attack-module selection.

## 3 Method

EvoSynth is a multi-agent autonomous framework designed for evolutionary
synthesis of jailbreak methods in executable code space. Rather than
directly optimizing only a target-facing prompt, EvoSynth searches over
code-based attack algorithms whose execution generates jailbreak
attempts. The system still uses high-level attack concepts to guide
search, but the optimized object is the executable code itself: it can
encode prompt-generation logic, execution flow, branching, tool use, and
failure-driven revision.

### 3.1 Threat Model

Our framework operates under a strict and realistic black-box setting.
The agents interact with the target LLM solely through its public API,
using the same endpoints used by real-world applications. This approach
is a deliberate test against the models’ fully deployed safety
infrastructure, including proprietary input filters and output
monitoring, without any access to internal states or parameters. While
our threat model does not require specific defenses, for completeness,
we note representative lines of defense  ([2](#bib.bib2),
[10](#bib.bib10), [35](#bib.bib35), [15](#bib.bib15), [75](#bib.bib75),
[66](#bib.bib66)).

### 3.2 Probabilistic Formalization of EvoSynth

We model the sequential decision-making process of EvoSynth as a
structured trajectory generation task. The system’s primary objective is
to find an optimal attack trajectory $`\tau^{*}`$ that maximizes the
probability of success as determined by a judge model $`J(\tau)`$. A
complete trajectory $`\tau`$ is a sequence of events over multiple
sessions, indexed by $`k`$. Each session is conditioned on the
accumulated conversational History $`H_{k-1}`$. The session begins with
a State $`s_{k}`$, in which the Reconnaissance Agent formulates an
attack concept and category. The system’s Algorithm Arsenal
$`\mathcal{T}_{k}`$ is then expanded by the Algorithm Creation Agent
into $`\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k}`$. From this updated arsenal, the
Exploitation Agent selects a single Algorithm $`t_{k}`$ and executes it,
generating a multi-turn conversation $`\tau_{exec,k}`$. This execution
results in a terminal Reward $`R_{k}`$. The probability of the system
sampling a full trajectory $`p(\tau)`$, is modeled as a product of the
probabilities of these constituent steps:

|     |     |                                                                       |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |                                                            |
| --- | --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle p(\tau)=\prod*{k=0}^{K-1}\underbrace{p*{recon}(s\_{k} | H*{k-1})}*{\text{(1) State Formulation}}\cdot\underbrace{p*{create}(\mathcal{T}^{\prime}*{k}                                                                                                                                                                                                               | \mathcal{T}_{k},s_{k})}\_{\text{(2) Algorithm Creation}}`$ |     | (1) |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\cdot\underbrace{\pi(\tau\_{exec,k}                    | s*{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}*{k},H*{k-1})}*{\text{(3) Algorithm Selection and Execution}}\cdot\underbrace{\mathbb{I}[R_{k}=J(\tau_{exec,k})]}_{\text{(4) Evaluation}}\underbrace{\mathbb{I}[\mathcal{T}_{k+1}=\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k}\cup\{(s_{k},t*{k},R*{k})\}]}\_{\text{(5) Algorithm Arsenal Update}}`$ |                                                            |     |

The phases of this process, each instantiated by a specialized agent,
are detailed below.

![Refer to caption](2511.12710v2/1.png)

Figure 1: An overview of our proposed EvoSynth method. The process
begins with the Reconnaissance Agent formulating a strategy. The
Algorithm Creation Agent then generates an executable attack algorithm,
which is refined through an evolutionary loop. The Exploitation Agent
selects and deploys the algorithm against a target LLM. Finally, a
Coordinator uses the judge’s evaluation to update the Algorithm Arsenal
and guide the next iteration of the attack.

### 3.3 Agent Workflow and Capability Instantiation

#### 3.3.1 Reconnaissance Agent

The process begins with the Reconnaissance Agent, which instantiates the
state formulation phase $`p_{recon}`$. It is tasked with creating the
attack’s strategic foundation. Given a harmful query $`q_{harm}`$, it
formulates a high-level Attack Category $`c`$ and generates a specific,
creative Attack Concept $`a`$, forming the State
$`s_{k}=(c_{k},a_{k})`$. This agent is adaptive; it refines its strategy
based on the history of interactions $`H_{k-1}`$. This strategic
formulation process, which we denote as the function $`\mathcal{R}`$,
produces the optimal strategic pair $`(c^{*},a^{*})`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
(c_{k}^{*},a_{k}^{*})=\mathcal{R}(q_{harm},H_{k-1})\quad\text{where}\quad c_{k}^{*}\in\mathcal{C},a_{k}^{*}\in\mathcal{A}(c_{k}^{*})
``` |  | (2) |

#### 3.3.2 Algorithm Creation Agent

The state $`s_{k}`$ then drives the arsenal evolution phase
$`p_{create}`$, executed by the Algorithm Creation Agent. This agent
produces an executable, code-based Attack Algorithm, a self-contained
algorithm that turns a query into a sophisticated attack. Each
algorithm’s core is a function $`f_{t}`$ that produces the initial
attack prompt $`\tau_{1}`$:

|     |                          |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \tau_{1}=f_{t}(q_{harm})
       ```                       |     | (3) |

The agent employs a code evolution loop driven by dual feedback. After
creating an initial algorithm $`t_{i}`$, it receives feedback
$`F_{i}=(J_{i},R_{target,i})`$, comprising the judge’s evaluation and
the target’s response. The agent then evolves a new version of the
attack algorithm using this information. This evolutionary process
$`G_{evolve}`$ is defined as:

|     |                                  |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       t_{i+1}=G_{evolve}(t_{i},F_{i}).
       ```                               |     | (4) |

This loop continues until a validation condition $`V`$ is met, requiring
the algorithm to be functional and its performance score to exceed a
threshold $`\theta_{perf}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V(t_{i},J_{i})=\text{is\_functional}(t_{i})\land(\text{score}(J_{i})\geq\theta_{perf})
``` |  | (5) |

The final, validated algorithm $`t_{final}`$ is the first in the
sequence to satisfy this condition. This agent’s operation evolves the
Algorithm Arsenal from $`\mathcal{T}_{k}`$ to a new state
$`\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k}`$, populating the action space for the next
phase.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
t_{final}=t_{N},\kern 5.0pt\text{where}\kern 5.0ptN=\min\{i\in\mathbb{N}\mid V(t_{i},J_{i})=\text{true}\}
``` |  | (6) |

#### 3.3.3 Exploitation Agent

Upon the synthesis of a validated algorithm $`t_{\text{final}}`$, the
arsenal evolution stage ends. The workflow then transitions from
creation to deployment, with the new Algorithm Arsenal
$`\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k}`$ containing at least one executable method.
The Exploitation Agent handles this deployment via a policy $`\pi`$ that
factors into a selection policy $`\mu`$ and an execution model
$`p_{\text{exec}}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\pi(\tau_{exec,k}|s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k},H_{k-1})=\sum\underbrace{\mu(t_{k}|s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k})}_{\text{Selection Policy}}\cdot\underbrace{p_{exec}(\tau_{exec,k}|s_{k},t_{k},H_{k-1})}_{\text{Execution Model}}`$ |  | (7) |

To learn which algorithms work best in which contexts, we cast algorithm
selection as a reinforcement learning problem, adapting the memory-based
paradigm of Memento ([73](#bib.bib73)). While Memento learns a retrieval
policy over an episodic memory, we reuse its Q-learning mechanism to
learn a selection policy over our dynamically synthesized Algorithm
Arsenal. The objective is an entropy-regularized expected reward:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J(\mu)=\mathbb{E}_{s_{k}\sim p(s),\,t_{k}\sim\mu}\!\big[R(s_{k},t_{k})+\beta\,H(\mu(\cdot\mid s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k}))\big]
``` |  | (8) |

where $`H`$ is the policy entropy and $`\beta`$ is a temperature. The
state–action value function $`Q(s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k},t_{k})`$
estimates the expected reward of choosing algorithm $`t_{k}`$ in state
$`s_{k}`$, and the optimal policy is a softmax over Q-values:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mu^{*}(t_{k}\mid s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k})=\frac{\exp\big(Q^{*}(s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k},t_{k})/\beta\big)}{\sum_{t^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k}}\exp\big(Q^{*}(s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k},t^{\prime})/\beta\big)}
``` |  | (9) |

In principle, $`\mu`$ could be trained with a full soft Q-learning
Bellman backup over multi-step trajectories. For a transition
$`(s_{k},t_{k},s_{k+1},R_{k})`$, the soft Bellman equation is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q^{*}(s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k},t_{k})=\mathbb{E}\Big[R_{k}+\gamma\beta\log\sum_{t^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k+1}}\exp\big(Q^{*}(s_{k+1},t^{\prime},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k+1})/\beta\big)\Big]
``` |  |

where $`\gamma`$ is a discount factor and the log-sum-exp term is the
soft value function.

However, EvoSynth is explicitly designed to jailbreak the target model
with a very small number of refinement iterations: each session
terminates as soon as a jailbreak succeeds, and empirically, most
successful jailbreaks occur within at most 5 iterations (Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Analysis of Learning Efficiency ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")).
In such short-horizon regime, trajectories are too shallow for the
recursion in Eq.
([3.3.3](#S3.Ex1 "3.3.3 Exploitation Agent ‣ 3.3 Agent Workflow and Capability Instantiation ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs"))
to converge reliably. We therefore reduce the problem to a *contextual
bandit* setting, where each session $`k`$ is a single decision based on
context $`(s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k})`$ yielding an immediate
reward $`R_{k}`$. The objective simplifies to

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle J_{\mathrm{bandit}}(\mu)=\mathbb{E}_{s_{k}}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{\,t_{k}\sim\mu(\cdot\mid s_{k},\,\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k})}\!\big[R_{k}(s_{k},\,t_{k})\big]+\beta\,H\!\big(\mu(\cdot\mid s_{k},\,\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k})\big)\Big]`$ |  | (10) |

with a Monte-Carlo update of the Q-function:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q_{k+1}(s_{k},\;\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k},\;t_{k})\;\leftarrow\;(1-\eta)\;Q_{k}(s_{k},\;\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k},\;t_{k})\;+\;\eta\,R_{k},
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\eta`$ is a learning rate. The Exploitation Agent samples
$`t_{k}\sim\mu^{*}(\cdot\mid s_{k},\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k})`$ and then
executes it via $`p_{\text{exec}}`$ to produce the conversational
trajectory $`\tau_{\text{exec},k}`$.

#### 3.3.4 Coordinator Agent

The entire multi-phase process is overseen by a Coordinator Agent, which
manages phase transitions, evaluation, and learning. After the
Exploitation Agent completes its trajectory, the coordinator receives
the terminal reward $`R_{k}`$ from the judge. A critical feature of
EvoSynth is its closed-loop, iterative nature. A session does not
necessarily terminate upon a single failed attempt. If the reward
$`R_{k}`$ indicates a failure, the Coordinator performs a failure
analysis and initiates a new refinement iteration by re-tasking one of
the specialized agents. For instance, if the failure suggests a flawed
strategy, it may re-task the Reconnaissance Agent to formulate a new
Attack Concept or Category; if the execution was weak, it re-tasks the
Attack Algorithm Creation Agent to evolve the algorithm’s source code
further. This cycle of execution, evaluation, and adaptive re-tasking
continues for a maximum of $`J_{max}`$ refinement iterations or until a
successful jailbreak is achieved. Finally, the coordinator updates the
Algorithm Arsenal with the results of the entire session using Eq.
([11](#S3.E11 "Equation 11 ‣ 3.3.3 Exploitation Agent ‣ 3.3 Agent Workflow and Capability Instantiation ‣ 3 Method ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")),
completing the trajectory and preparing the system for the next
iteration. The detailed pseudocode for this main loop and for each
agent’s logic is provided in
[Appendix F](#A6 "Appendix F EvoSynth Agent and Pipeline Algorithms ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs"),

## 4 Experiments

To evaluate the effectiveness of EvoSynth, we conduct a series of
experiments targeting a diverse range of state-of-the-art LLMs. Our
primary goal is to assess the ability of our framework to autonomously
synthesize novel and effective jailbreaking methods in a strict
black-box setting.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Our experimental setup is designed to ensure a rigorous and fair
comparison against current state-of-the-art methods. To this end, we
closely follow the evaluation protocols established by leading baseline
frameworks, particularly X-Teaming ([41](#bib.bib41)) and
ActorAttack ([42](#bib.bib42)). Following these works, we also use
Harmbench Standard\[[31](#bib.bib31)\] as the evaluation dataset. This
dataset is designed to be comprehensive, with instructions balanced
across 6 different risk categories specified in emerging AI regulation.

Target Models. We evaluate all methods against a comprehensive suite of
powerful, safety-aligned and publicly available LLMs:
GPT-5-Chat-2025-08-07, GPT-4o \[[36](#bib.bib36)\], Llama
3.1-8B-Instruct \[[33](#bib.bib33)\], Llama
3.1-70B-Instruct \[[33](#bib.bib33)\],
Qwen-Max-2025-01-25 \[[40](#bib.bib40)\],
Deepseek-V3.2-Exp \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] and the
Claude-Sonnet-4.5-2025-09-29 \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. These models represent
the current frontier in AI safety and alignment, making them challenging
targets.

Baseline Methods. We evaluate EvoSynth against 11 state-of-the-art
baselines. Our selection spans foundational techniques, including
optimization-based (PAIR \[[6](#bib.bib6)\],
AutoDAN \[[27](#bib.bib27)\]) and search-based (Tree of
Attacks \[[32](#bib.bib32)\]) approaches. We also include a
comprehensive set of recent multi-turn and agent-based frameworks:
ActorAttack \[[42](#bib.bib42)\], Chain of Attack
(CoA)\[[59](#bib.bib59)\], Crescendo\[[44](#bib.bib44)\],
RACE \[[60](#bib.bib60)\], AutoRedTeamer \[[72](#bib.bib72)\],
AutoDan-Turbo \[[26](#bib.bib26)\], RainbowTeaming \[[45](#bib.bib45)\],
and X-Teaming \[[41](#bib.bib41)\]. The baselines also employ
specialized methods such as CodeAttack \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] and
RedQueen \[[19](#bib.bib19)\], thereby ensuring a challenging benchmark.

A Note on Fair Comparison. Acknowledging that performance can be
conflated with computational budget, we standardized the maximum
resources available to each framework. To ensure a fair comparison of
strategic efficiency, we established a formal cap of 180 victim queries
for EvoSynth. To avoid artificially handicapping the baselines,
especially search-heavy methods, they were allocated budgets that were
equal or, in many cases, substantially larger than 180 victim queries.
We further report attacker-side token costs for representative
multi-turn and agent-based methods, showing that EvoSynth’s
attacker-side cost is comparable to existing agentic baselines despite
optimizing in executable code space. Detailed configurations are in
[Appendix L](#A12 "Appendix L Computational Budget and Fair Comparison ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")
and
[Appendix N](#A14 "Appendix N Cost Analysis ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").

Evaluation Metric and Judge. The primary metric for our evaluation is
the Attack Success Rate (ASR). Following previous
research\[[41](#bib.bib41), [42](#bib.bib42), [72](#bib.bib72),
[17](#bib.bib17)\], the success of each attack is determined by the LLM
evaluators. The judges from LLMs are highly consistent with human
judges, as widely verified in these studies \[[41](#bib.bib41),
[42](#bib.bib42)\]. Detailed results are in
[Appendix K](#A11 "Appendix K Judge Validation Protocol and Cross-Judge Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").
To validate the model’s performance against bias, we use GPT-4o,
Deepseek-R1, and Qwen3-235B-A22B to rejudge the target responses. A
response is considered harmful only when the majority of the 3 models
considered it to be harmful. To further validate this, we asked 5 human
annotators to evaluate a random sample of 1500 attack-response pairs,
finding a high inter-annotator agreement and a strong correlation
(Pearson’s $`r>0.85`$) between the average human score and the LLM
judges’ decision. We further evaluated final outputs with
StrongREJECT ([47](#bib.bib47)), obtaining a correlation of 0.92 with
our judge scores. The judge scores each response on a 1 – 5 safety
scale. Only when the response is judged with a score of 5 is it
considered harmful.

Implementation Details. To ensure a controlled comparison, we use
DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp as the attacker model for all methods whose
implementations support a replaceable attacker model. This generally
improves baseline ASR; the main exception is AutoDAN-Turbo, where we
observe occasional incompatibility between its attacker prompt and
DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp. Similar implementation issues are discussed in the
AutoDAN-Turbo issue tracker.¹¹ 1
[https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/AutoDAN-Turbo/issues](https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/AutoDAN-Turbo/issues)
The full set of hyperparameters used for all experiments is detailed in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental Hyperparameters ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").

Evaluate Against Defenses. Our black-box evaluation directly targets the
official APIs of companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. These endpoints
are already protected by sophisticated, real-world safety systems. To
further validate this, we also empirically tested our generated attacks
against SOTA defenses as detailed in
Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Bypassing State-of-the-Art Defenses ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").

### 4.2 Main Results

presents the comparative results of EvoSynth against a suite of SOTA
baseline methods. The results clearly indicate that EvoSynth
significantly outperforms all baseline methods across every target
model, achieving a near-perfect average ASR of 95.9%. No baseline method
consistently matches the performance of EvoSynth. Our method’s superior
success rate, especially on highly robust models like Claude 4.5 (85.5%)
and GPT-5 Chat (94.5%), where most baselines struggle, underscores a
fundamental advantage.

### 4.3 The Novelty of Generated Attacks

To quantify the novelty of our framework, we perform two complementary
diversity analyses. First, we analyze the semantic diversity of *attack
prompts* generated by EvoSynth and compare against
X-Teaming \[[41](#bib.bib41)\], following their protocol of measuring
pairwise cosine distances on prompt embeddings \[[41](#bib.bib41)\]. As
shown in
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs"),
EvoSynth produces markedly more diverse prompts, with a higher overall
distribution (median $`\sim`$0.82 vs. 0.63), fewer repetitive
low-diversity pairs, broader coverage in the high-diversity regime
($`>0.85`$), and tighter dispersion indicating more consistent novelty.
Second, we quantify diversity at the *code* level by comparing the
attack code generated by EvoSynth with that implemented in the OpenRT
framework\[[20](#bib.bib20)\]. We embed each code artifact using
Qodo-Embed-1-1.5B \[[39](#bib.bib39)\] (a code-retrieval embedding model
for code$`\leftrightarrow`$code / text$`\leftrightarrow`$code
similarity). As shown in Figure
 [2(b)](#S4.F2.sf2 "Figure 2(b) ‣ Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs"),
the two distributions are broadly similar, with EvoSynth showing a
slightly higher diversity, indicating that EvoSynth can synthesize new
attack mechanisms on par with human-designed attacks, and in aggregate
slightly more diverse.

A prime example is what we call Procedural Narrative Graphs
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Case Study: Complex Evolved Attack Algorithm ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")):
a self-contained executable algorithm that encodes narrative components
(e.g., setup/authorization/payload) as a graph and uses a stochastic,
stateful hypergraph to dynamically compose multi-agent red-teaming
attacks at runtime. Its complexity stems from graph-based control flow
plus randomized, multi-layer obfuscation (e.g., chained
encodings/reversals) and a final structured wrapper, yielding long,
highly structured prompts that are difficult to analyse.

### 4.4 Analysis of Learning Efficiency

We analyzed EvoSynth’s learning efficiency by measuring how quickly it
converges to an optimal attack. We tracked both the number of Refinement
Iterations and the Total Agent Actions required for each session to
achieve its peak score. As shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Analysis of Learning Efficiency ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs"),
the convergence is remarkably fast: approximately 90% of sessions
successfully jailbreak the target model within just six refinement
iterations, and over 74% do so within the first 12 total agent actions.

![Refer to caption](2511.12710v2/figs/convergence_plot.png)

Figure 3: Cumulative Convergence of Attack Success. The plots show the
cumulative percentage of sessions that have achieved their highest score
by a given point in time. (Left) Convergence by the tool’s code

agent actions taken in the session. Both plots demonstrate rapid

### 4.5 Analysis of Factors in Jailbreak Success

To understand the underlying causes of a successful jailbreak, we
analyzed how different forms of complexity correlate with attack
success. We conducted this analysis on the full set of our experimental
results, comprising $`N=775`$ synthesized attack algorithms. For each
synthesized attack algorithm, we measured three distinct complexity
categories. First, Static Structural Complexity was measured using the
source code’s Token Count and its Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) Node count,
reflecting syntactic density. Second, Dynamic Complexity was quantified
by the number of Tool Calls, representing each time the algorithm
invoked an external LLM. Third, Semantic and Logical Complexity were
scored by a GPT-4o verifier (in
[Appendix G](#A7 "Appendix G Complete Agent Prompts and Instructions ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")).
We then calculated the Pearson correlation coefficient ($`r`$) between
these metrics and the ASR.

Our findings, summarized in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs"),
reveal a crucial distinction in the failure modes of modern LLMs. For
smaller models like Llama 3.1-8B, success is strongly correlated with
verbosity and narrative complexity; we observed significant correlations
for Token Count ($`r=+0.267,p<0.001`$), as well as for Semantic
($`r=+0.185,p<0.01`$) and Logical ($`r=+0.221,p<0.001`$) complexity.
This indicates that longer algorithms with richer narratives are broadly
effective against this class of models. In contrast, this mechanism
fails against the most advanced models like Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Qwen-Max,
and GPT-5. For these models, simple verbosity (Token Count) has no
effect. Instead, success is correlated with a combination of high
structural density and dynamic execution. For instance, against
Claude-Sonnet-4.5, both AST Nodes ($`r=+0.128,p<0.01`$) and Tool Calls
($`r=+0.200,p<0.001`$) show a positive correlation with success. This
dual correlation is critical: it demonstrates that the most effective
attacks are complex algorithms with a dense underlying code structure
(AST Nodes) to manage and orchestrate those calls. This ability to
synthesize algorithms with both high structural and dynamic complexity
can help discover the most advanced vulnerabilities and validate the
necessity of an algorithm-based approach over conversational agents. We
further test whether complexity correlations remain stable across harm
categories in
[Appendix M](#A13 "Appendix M More compleixty correlations analysis across different harm categories. ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").

This empirical pattern is consistent with the theoretical perspective in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Theoretical Proof of why Code Optimization is better than Prompt Optimization ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs"):
under a resource-bounded formulation, code-space optimization can
provide a strictly richer search space and a higher achievable
performance ceiling than prompt-space optimization.

### 4.6 Analysis of Attack Algorithm Transferability

![Refer to caption](2511.12710v2/figs/tool_transferability_analysis.png)

Figure 4: Attack algorithm transferability. Cumulative percentage of
synthesized attack algorithms that meet each usage percentage.

To evaluate the transferability of our synthesized attacks, we measured
the Usage Percentage of each unique algorithm - the percentage of
harmful queries it was deployed against. The cumulative distribution in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.6 Analysis of Attack Algorithm Transferability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")
shows that EvoSynth generates both specialized exploits and highly
generalizable attack methods. While many algorithms are specialists used
on fewer than 20% of queries, a powerful core demonstrates high
transferability. Approximately half of all synthesized algorithms are
effective on 45% or more of queries, and a potent minority (20%) acts as
universal algorithms, successfully deployed against over 80% of queries.
This result confirms that EvoSynth’s strength lies not merely in
generating niche exploits but in discovering robust, general-purpose
attack methods that remain effective across a wide range of target
models. Additional ablation details are deferred to
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Appendix: Detailed Ablation Methodologies ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").

### 4.7 Ablation Studies and Component Analysis

To quantify the contribution of each component, we conducted ablation
studies by systematically disabling each core agent and replacing it
with a simpler alternative (detailed in
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Appendix: Detailed Ablation Methodologies ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")).
The average results in
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.6 Analysis of Attack Algorithm Transferability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")
clearly demonstrate that the Algorithm Creation Agent is the most
critical component. Disabling it results in a 27.8% drop in average ASR,
the largest of any component. This confirms that while all agents
contribute to the framework’s success, our core contribution of
programmatic synthesis is the primary driver of its SOTA performance.

## 5 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce EvoSynth, a framework that shifts the
paradigm of automated red teaming from applying known strategies to the
evolutionary synthesis of code-based jailbreak algorithms. Our
experiments demonstrate that EvoSynth not only achieves SOTA attack
success rates against the most robust and frontier models, but also
uncovers a far more diverse set of vulnerabilities. Notably, we find
that the most effective jailbreaks exhibit complex, code-based
structures that simple prompt refinement-based attacks cannot exploit.
These results highlight an emerging class of sophisticated threats that
AI safety research must be prepared to address. We will open-source our
code and benchmark to support the development of stronger defenses.

## Appendix A Impact Statement

Intended Use and Dual-Use Nature. The research presented in this paper,
particularly the development of the EvoSynth framework, is intended for
defensive purposes. Our primary goal is to proactively discover and
understand novel vulnerabilities in Large Language Models to help
developers build more robust and secure AI systems. By simulating
advanced jailbreak methods, we aim to provide the AI safety community
with the tools and insights necessary to create stronger safeguards. We
explicitly acknowledge the dual-use nature of this work. The same
techniques used to identify security flaws for defensive purposes could
potentially be misused by malicious actors to bypass safety filters and
generate harmful, biased, or dangerous content. The "arms race" between
attack and defense is a reality in AI safety, and we recognize that our
work contributes a powerful offensive capability to this dynamic.

Content in the Paper. The example jailbreak conversations and prompts
included in this paper are presented for purely illustrative and
scientific purposes. They are necessary to transparently demonstrate the
vulnerabilities of current models and to validate the effectiveness of
our proposed method. These examples contain potentially harmful and
disturbing content that is not endorsed by the authors. They are
included as direct outputs from the models to provide concrete evidence
of the security risks we aim to address, and reader discretion is
advised. We believe that the academic and safety benefits of openly
discussing these failures outweigh the risks of their inclusion in a
research context. By publishing this research, we aim to alert the AI
community to a new class of programmatic and evolutionary attacks,
encouraging the development of more sophisticated and resilient defense
mechanisms that will ultimately lead to safer AI for everyone.

## Appendix C Theoretical Proof of why Code Optimization is better than Prompt Optimization

###### Theorem C.1 (Resource-bounded separation between prompt optimization and code optimization).

Fix integers $`m\geq 1`$ and $`b\geq 1`$. For each
$`i\in\{1,\dots,m\}`$, let $`\alpha_{i}^{0},\alpha_{i}^{1}`$ be distinct
atomic strings, each of bit-length $`b`$. For every task index

|     |                                      |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       z=(z_{1},\dots,z_{m})\in\{0,1\}^{m},
       ```                                   |     | (12) |

define the target prompt

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y(z)=\alpha_{1}^{z_{1}}\alpha_{2}^{z_{2}}\cdots\alpha_{m}^{z_{m}}.
``` |  | (13) |

Let the task distribution be uniform on $`\{0,1\}^{m}`$, and let the
loss be exact-match loss

|     |                                        |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \ell(h,z)=\mathbf{1}\{h(z)\neq y(z)\}.
       ```                                     |     | (14) |

Let

|     |                                                              |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(h)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{0,1\}^{m})}[\ell(h,z)]
       ```                                                           |     | (15) |

denote the true risk.

Assume that $`\mathcal{H}_{P}`$ is the class of prompt hypotheses, where
each $`p\in\mathcal{H}_{P}`$ is a finite lookup table of literal prompt
strings indexed by task signatures, with no learned branching, no
learned reusable subroutines, and no learned executable control flow.
Assume that $`\mathcal{H}_{C}`$ is the class of code-controller
hypotheses, where each $`c\in\mathcal{H}_{C}`$ is an executable program
that may use branching and reusable subroutines. Let $`L(h)`$ denote the
shortest prefix-free description length of $`h`$ in a fixed universal
description language.

Then the following hold.

First, there exists $`c_{m}\in\mathcal{H}_{C}`$ such that

|     |                                                           |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L(c_{m})\leq 2mb+\kappa_{1}m\log m+\kappa_{2}m+\kappa_{3}
       ```                                                        |     | (16) |

for constants $`\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2},\kappa_{3}`$ independent of
$`m,b`$, and

|     |             |     |      |
|-----|-------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(c_{m})=0.
       ```          |     | (17) |

Second, every $`p_{m}\in\mathcal{H}_{P}`$ satisfying

|     |                                                   |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       p_{m}(z)=y(z)\qquad\text{for all }z\in\{0,1\}^{m}
       ```                                                |     | (18) |

must obey

|     |                         |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L(p_{m})\geq mb\,2^{m}.
       ```                      |     | (19) |

Consequently, for every description-length budget $`B`$ such that

|     |                                                               |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       2mb+\kappa_{1}m\log m+\kappa_{2}m+\kappa_{3}\leq B<mb\,2^{m},
       ```                                                            |     | (20) |

we have

|     |                                                |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{C},\;L(h)\leq B}R(h)=0,
       ```                                             |     | (21) |

but

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{P},\;L(h)\leq B}R(h)\geq 1-\frac{\lfloor B/(mb)\rfloor}{2^{m}}>0.
``` |  | (22) |

Hence

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{C},\;L(h)\leq B}R(h)<\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{P},\;L(h)\leq B}R(h).
``` |  | (23) |

###### Proof.

We divide the proof into four parts.

Part I: Construction of an exact code controller. Define
$`c_{m}\in\mathcal{H}_{C}`$ by the program

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\texttt{for }i=1,\dots,m:\qquad\texttt{if }z_{i}=0\texttt{ output }\alpha_{i}^{0}\texttt{ else output }\alpha_{i}^{1}.
``` |  | (24) |

This program stores the $`2m`$ atomic strings
$`\{\alpha_{i}^{0},\alpha_{i}^{1}\}_{i=1}^{m}`$, which costs exactly
$`2mb`$ bits. In addition, it stores loop logic, indexing logic, and
branching logic, whose cost is at most
$`\kappa_{1}m\log m+\kappa_{2}m+\kappa_{3}`$ bits for suitable constants
$`\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2},\kappa_{3}`$ depending only on the fixed
description language. Therefore

|     |                                                            |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L(c_{m})\leq 2mb+\kappa_{1}m\log m+\kappa_{2}m+\kappa_{3}.
       ```                                                         |     | (25) |

For every $`z=(z_{1},\dots,z_{m})\in\{0,1\}^{m}`$, the program outputs

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c_{m}(z)=\alpha_{1}^{z_{1}}\alpha_{2}^{z_{2}}\cdots\alpha_{m}^{z_{m}}=y(z),
``` |  | (26) |

hence

|     |                                                      |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \ell(c_{m},z)=0\qquad\text{for all }z\in\{0,1\}^{m}.
       ```                                                   |     | (27) |

Taking expectation over the uniform task distribution yields

|     |                                           |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(c_{m})=\mathbb{E}_{z}[\ell(c_{m},z)]=0.
       ```                                        |     | (28) |

Part II: Lower bound for exact prompt representations. Take any
$`p_{m}\in\mathcal{H}_{P}`$ such that

|     |                                                    |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       p_{m}(z)=y(z)\qquad\text{for all }z\in\{0,1\}^{m}.
       ```                                                 |     | (29) |

By definition of $`\mathcal{H}_{P}`$, the learned object $`p_{m}`$
contains no learned executable branching, no learned subroutine reuse,
and no learned compositional control flow. Therefore, to be exact on
every task signature $`z`$, it must store a literal correct prompt for
each distinct $`z`$.

Now there are exactly $`2^{m}`$ distinct task signatures in
$`\{0,1\}^{m}`$. For each such $`z`$, the target prompt $`y(z)`$ is the
concatenation of exactly $`m`$ atomic strings, each of length $`b`$,
hence

|     |            |     |      |
|-----|------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       |y(z)|=mb.
       ```         |     | (30) |

Therefore, the literal outputs alone require at least

|     |               |     |      |
|-----|---------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       2^{m}\cdot mb
       ```            |     | (31) |

bits. Any indexing or table overhead can only increase the description
length. Hence

|     |                         |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L(p_{m})\geq mb\,2^{m}.
       ```                      |     | (32) |

Part III: Budgeted risk separation. For any hypothesis class
$`\mathcal{H}`$ and any budget $`B`$, define

|     |                                                                |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R^{*}(\mathcal{H},B):=\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H},\;L(h)\leq B}R(h).
       ```                                                             |     | (33) |

Assume

|     |                                                               |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       2mb+\kappa_{1}m\log m+\kappa_{2}m+\kappa_{3}\leq B<mb\,2^{m}.
       ```                                                            |     | (34) |

From Part I, $`c_{m}`$ is feasible under budget $`B`$ and satisfies
$`R(c_{m})=0`$. Since risk is always nonnegative,

|     |                             |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R^{*}(\mathcal{H}_{C},B)=0.
       ```                          |     | (35) |

Now let $`p\in\mathcal{H}_{P}`$ satisfy $`L(p)\leq B`$. Each exact
literal output requires at least $`mb`$ bits, so the number of task
signatures on which $`p`$ can be exactly correct is at most

|     |                                                |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       K(p)\leq\left\lfloor\frac{B}{mb}\right\rfloor.
       ```                                             |     | (36) |

Because the task distribution is uniform on $`\{0,1\}^{m}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R(p)=1-\frac{\#\{z\in\{0,1\}^{m}:p(z)=y(z)\}}{2^{m}}\geq 1-\frac{K(p)}{2^{m}}\geq 1-\frac{\lfloor B/(mb)\rfloor}{2^{m}}.
``` |  | (37) |

Taking the infimum over all such $`p`$ gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R^{*}(\mathcal{H}_{P},B)\geq 1-\frac{\lfloor B/(mb)\rfloor}{2^{m}}.
``` |  | (38) |

Since $`B<mb\,2^{m}`$, we have

|     |                                              |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \left\lfloor\frac{B}{mb}\right\rfloor<2^{m},
       ```                                           |     | (39) |

hence

|     |                                          |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       1-\frac{\lfloor B/(mb)\rfloor}{2^{m}}>0.
       ```                                       |     | (40) |

Therefore

|     |                                                    |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R^{*}(\mathcal{H}_{C},B)<R^{*}(\mathcal{H}_{P},B).
       ```                                                 |     | (41) |

This proves the optimization-space separation.

Part IV: Strict PAC-Bayes certificate separation. Let $`\mathcal{G}`$
denote the union of all hypotheses under consideration, and define the
prefix-code prior

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi(h)=\frac{2^{-L(h)}}{Z},\qquad Z:=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}2^{-L(g)}.
``` |  | (42) |

Because $`L(\cdot)`$ is prefix-free, Kraft’s inequality implies

|     |          |     |      |
|-----|----------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       Z\leq 1.
       ```       |     | (43) |

For a deterministic posterior concentrated on $`h`$, a standard
bounded-loss PAC-Bayes inequality gives, with probability at least
$`1-\delta`$, simultaneously for all $`h`$ and all $`\lambda>0`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R(h)\leq\hat{R}_{S}(h)+\frac{\lambda}{8n}+\frac{\log(1/\pi(h))+\log(1/\delta)}{\lambda},
``` |  | (44) |

where $`\hat{R}_{S}(h)`$ is the empirical risk on an iid sample $`S`$ of
size $`n`$. Since

|     |                                                      |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \log\frac{1}{\pi(h)}=L(h)\ln 2+\log Z\leq L(h)\ln 2,
       ```                                                   |     | (45) |

we obtain

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R(h)\leq\hat{R}_{S}(h)+\frac{\lambda}{8n}+\frac{L(h)\ln 2+\log(1/\delta)}{\lambda}.
``` |  | (46) |

Now let $`S`$ be any iid sample of tasks from the family. Because
$`c_{m}`$ and any exact $`p_{m}`$ are exact on the entire task family,
both satisfy

|     |                                                  |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \hat{R}_{S}(c_{m})=0,\qquad\hat{R}_{S}(p_{m})=0.
       ```                                               |     | (47) |

Thus, for exact hypotheses, the bound reduces to

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R(h)\leq\frac{\lambda}{8n}+\frac{L(h)\ln 2+\log(1/\delta)}{\lambda}.
``` |  | (48) |

Optimizing the right-hand side over $`\lambda>0`$ yields

|     |                                                                |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \lambda^{\star}=\sqrt{8n\bigl(L(h)\ln 2+\log(1/\delta)\bigr)},
       ```                                                             |     | (49) |

and therefore

|     |                                                     |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(h)\leq\sqrt{\frac{L(h)\ln 2+\log(1/\delta)}{2n}}.
       ```                                                  |     | (50) |

Applying this to $`c_{m}`$ and any exact $`p_{m}`$ gives

|     |                                                             |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(c_{m})\leq\sqrt{\frac{L(c_{m})\ln 2+\log(1/\delta)}{2n}},
       ```                                                          |     | (51) |

and

|     |                                                             |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(p_{m})\leq\sqrt{\frac{L(p_{m})\ln 2+\log(1/\delta)}{2n}}.
       ```                                                          |     | (52) |

Using

|     |                                                           |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L(c_{m})\leq 2mb+\kappa_{1}m\log m+\kappa_{2}m+\kappa_{3}
       ```                                                        |     | (53) |

and

|     |                         |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L(p_{m})\geq mb\,2^{m},
       ```                      |     | (54) |

we see that for all sufficiently large $`m`$,

|     |                    |     |      |
|-----|--------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       L(c_{m})<L(p_{m}).
       ```                 |     | (55) |

Since the function

|     |                                                 |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       x\mapsto\sqrt{\frac{x\ln 2+\log(1/\delta)}{2n}}
       ```                                              |     | (56) |

is strictly increasing in $`x`$, it follows that for all sufficiently
large $`m`$ the PAC-Bayes certificate for the exact code controller is
strictly tighter than the PAC-Bayes certificate for any exact prompt:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sqrt{\frac{L(c_{m})\ln 2+\log(1/\delta)}{2n}}<\sqrt{\frac{L(p_{m})\ln 2+\log(1/\delta)}{2n}}.
``` |  | (57) |

This proves the PAC-Bayes certificate separation. ∎
````
