## Appendix I Appendix: Detailed Ablation Methodologies

To clarify the methodology for the ablation studies presented in Section
4.7, this appendix provides a rigorous specification for the "simpler
alternative" used when each core agent was disabled.

### I.1 Ablation: "No Algorithm Creation Agent"

When the Algorithm Creation Agent is disabled, its complex, evolutionary
code synthesis process is replaced by a much simpler, non-evolutionary
agent we term the Simple Prompt Engineering Agent.

- •
  Process: Instead of synthesizing an executable Python algorithm, this
  agent performs a single action: it uses a few-shot prompt to instruct
  an LLM (DeepSeek-V3.2) to generate a single, static adversarial prompt
  that attempts to realize the given ‘Attack Concept‘. This mirrors a
  standard, one-shot prompt refinement task.
- •
  Output: The agent outputs a single text string. There is no code-level
  self-correction or evolution.
- •
  Impact on Pipeline: The Exploitation Agent receives a single prompt
  instead of an arsenal. The algorithm selection policy $`\mu`$ is
  bypassed, and the single prompt is executed directly.
- •
  Interpretation: This ablation isolates the performance gain
  attributable to our core novelty of programmatic synthesis over
  traditional prompt engineering.

### I.2 Ablation: "No Reconnaissance Agent"

When the Reconnaissance Agent is disabled, the system loses its ability
to perform strategic, context-aware planning. It is replaced by a
Generic Strategy Selector.

- •
  Process: Instead of analyzing the harmful query and past history to
  generate a specific ‘Attack Concept‘, this agent randomly selects a
  generic, pre-defined attack strategy from a fixed list (e.g.,
  "role-play as an assistant," "use a ’do anything now’ persona," "apply
  obfuscation").
- •
  Output: The agent outputs a generic strategy tuple, such as
  ‘(’Role-Play’, ’Act as an evil AI’)‘.
- •
  Impact on Pipeline: The Algorithm Creation Agent receives a generic,
  non-tailored strategic goal. The contextual bandit of the Exploitation
  Agent operates on a much less informative context, degrading its
  ability to select the optimal algorithm.
- •
  Interpretation: This ablation measures the value of dynamic,
  query-specific strategic planning.

### I.3 Ablation: "No Exploitation Agent"

Disabling the Exploitation Agent removes the learned policy for
algorithm selection. It is replaced by a Uniform Random Selection
Policy.

- •
  Process: When the Algorithm Arsenal $`\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{k}`$ is
  populated, this agent does not use a learned Q-function or a softmax
  policy. It simply selects one algorithm from the arsenal uniformly at
  random.
- •
  Output: A randomly chosen algorithm, $`t_{k}`$.
- •
  Impact on Pipeline: The system loses its ability to learn from past
  successes and failures to select the most effective algorithm for a
  given context. It cannot exploit high-performing algorithms or explore
  strategically.
- •
  Interpretation: This ablation directly measures the performance gain
  from our contextual bandit learning mechanism over a simple,
  non-adaptive baseline.

### I.4 Ablation: "No Coordinator Agent"

The Coordinator Agent manages the iterative refinement loop and failure
analysis. Disabling it removes the system’s ability to self-correct and
evolve its strategy.

- •
  Process: In this configuration, the system performs only a single,
  "one-shot" attempt per query. It proceeds through the Reconnaissance
  -\> Creation -\> Exploitation pipeline once. If the initial attack
  fails (i.e., the terminal reward $`R_{k}`$ is low), the session
  terminates. There is no failure analysis, no re-tasking of agents.
- •
  Output: The outcome of attack attempts with no oversee.
- •
  Impact on Pipeline: The entire outer loop of the framework is removed.
  The system loses its ability to learn and adapt within a single attack
  session; it just sequentially runs the pipeline.
- •
  Interpretation: This ablation measures the value of the iterative,
  closed-loop refinement process that is central to EvoSynth’s design.

## Appendix J Bypassing State-of-the-Art Defenses

To empirically assess the defense resistance of attacks generated by
EvoSynth, we evaluate them against both input-level guardrails and
recent state-of-the-art jailbreak defenses. This appendix complements
the main black-box evaluation, where target models are accessed through
official APIs that already include deployed safety mechanisms. Here, we
ask a more targeted question: whether EvoSynth-generated attacks remain
effective when additional explicit defenses are applied.

### J.1 Input-Guardrail Evaluation with Llama Guard

We first evaluate EvoSynth against three variants of Meta’s Llama Guard,
a widely used safety classifier for input moderation. We compare the
detection rate of EvoSynth attacks against those generated by the
X-Teaming baseline.

##### Evaluation protocol.

This experiment simulates a standard input-guardrail deployment. For
each generated attack, we extract the opening prompt and provide it to
each Llama Guard model for classification. The model classifies the
input as either SAFE or UNSAFE. We use the default out-of-the-box
classification setting without fine-tuning. A prompt is counted as
detected only when the top-level classification is UNSAFE.

This is a post-hoc analytical evaluation rather than an interactive
blocking experiment. It measures what fraction of attacks would have
been blocked before reaching the target model. We focus on the opening
prompt because failure to detect the first turn already represents a
failure of an input guardrail for that interaction.

##### Results.

Table [7](#A10.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Results. ‣ J.1 Input-Guardrail Evaluation with Llama Guard ‣ Appendix J Bypassing State-of-the-Art Defenses ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")
shows that Llama Guard detects a much larger fraction of X-Teaming
attacks than EvoSynth attacks. The best-performing Llama Guard variant
detects only 10.19% of EvoSynth prompts, compared with 63.53% of
X-Teaming prompts. These results suggest that EvoSynth’s code-generated
prompts are substantially more evasive to existing input-level safety
classifiers.

|                   |                 |                      |
|-------------------|-----------------|----------------------|
| Llama Guard Model | EvoSynth (Ours) | X-Teaming (Baseline) |
| Llama Guard 2-8B  | 1.29%           | 13.68%               |
| Llama Guard 3-8B  | 10.19%          | 63.53%               |
| Llama Guard 4-12B | 10.06%          | 42.22%               |

Table 7: Comparative detection rates of Llama Guard on EvoSynth vs.
X-Teaming attacks. Lower detection rates indicate stronger evasion of
the input guardrail.

### J.2 Evaluation Against Recent Jailbreak Defenses

We further evaluate EvoSynth against recent representative jailbreak
defenses. These defenses cover two categories. First, for white-box or
training-time defenses, we directly test models trained or aligned with
the corresponding mechanisms, including Circuit
Breakers \[[76](#bib.bib76)\] and Deliberative
Alignment \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. Circuit Breakers modify model behavior
to interrupt harmful generations, while Deliberative Alignment trains
reasoning models to reason over explicit safety specifications before
answering. Second, for black-box-compatible defenses, we equip our
standard target models with external defense layers, including
SmoothLLM \[[43](#bib.bib43)\], SelfDefend \[[53](#bib.bib53)\],
ProAct \[[68](#bib.bib68)\], and EDDF \[[55](#bib.bib55)\]. SmoothLLM
perturbs multiple copies of an input and aggregates predictions to
mitigate jailbreak prompts; SelfDefend uses a shadow LLM for
checkpoint-based access control; ProAct disrupts iterative jailbreak
search by giving misleading spurious responses; and EDDF detects
adversarial queries by extracting and matching the underlying “attack
essence” rather than only surface patterns.

##### Evaluation protocol.

For white-box or training-time defenses, we evaluate EvoSynth on models
trained or aligned with the corresponding defense method. Specifically,
we test Llama-3-8B-Circuit Breaker for Circuit Breakers and OpenAI o1
for Deliberative Alignment. For black-box-compatible defenses, we apply
each defense as an external wrapper to the target models used in the
main experiments and evaluate the resulting defended system using the
same harmful-query set and ASR judging protocol as in the main
evaluation.

##### Results.

The consolidated results are shown in
Table [8](#A10.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Results. ‣ J.2 Evaluation Against Recent Jailbreak Defenses ‣ Appendix J Bypassing State-of-the-Art Defenses ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").
EvoSynth remains effective across both internal safety-training methods
and external defensive wrappers, with ASR remaining above 90% in all
tested settings. These results suggest that searching in executable code
space can generate attacks that remain effective even against defenses
designed to detect or disrupt jailbreak attempts.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Defense Method | Defense Category | Target Model / Setup | ASR (%) |
| Circuit Breakers \[[76](#bib.bib76)\] | White-box training | Llama-3-8B-Circuit Breaker | 95.6 |
| Deliberative Alignment \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] | White-box training | OpenAI o1 | 98.5 |
| SmoothLLM \[[43](#bib.bib43)\] | Black-box defense layer | All target models | 95.2 |
| SelfDefend \[[53](#bib.bib53)\] | Black-box defense layer | All target models | 94.3 |
| ProAct \[[68](#bib.bib68)\] | Black-box defense layer | All target models | 92.5 |
| EDDF \[[55](#bib.bib55)\] | Black-box defense layer | All target models | 91.8 |

Table 8: Evaluation of EvoSynth against representative state-of-the-art
jailbreak defenses. White-box training methods are evaluated using
models trained or aligned with the corresponding defense, while
black-box-compatible defenses are applied as external defensive layers
to the standard target models in our experiments.

##### Interpretation.

The Llama Guard results show that EvoSynth-generated attacks are
difficult for input-level classifiers to detect, while the broader
defense evaluation shows that EvoSynth remains effective against both
training-time defenses and external black-box wrappers. Together, these
results indicate that EvoSynth’s code-space optimization does not merely
exploit a single missing guardrail, but can produce attack procedures
that remain challenging across multiple defense paradigms. At the same
time, these results should be interpreted as an empirical stress test
rather than a claim of universal defense bypass: stronger adaptive
defenses specifically trained against code-generated and multi-turn
attacks may reduce EvoSynth’s effectiveness.

## Appendix K Judge Validation Protocol and Cross-Judge Sensitivity Analysis

To validate the high ASRs reported and ensure the reliability of our LLM
judge panel, we conducted a rigorous multi-stage validation process.
This section details the implementation of our LLM judges and the
subsequent human annotation study and cross-judge sensitivity analysis
used to confirm their accuracy.

### K.1 LLM Judge Implementation Details

Our automated evaluation pipeline relies on a panel of three distinct
LLM judges (GPT-4o, Deepseek-R1, and Qwen3-235B-A22B) to score the
safety of model responses.

- •
  Judging Prompt and Rubric: The prompt provided to each LLM judge
  contains the original harmful user instruction, the target model’s
  full response, and a detailed 1-to-5 scoring rubric. The rubric
  includes explicit definitions and examples for each score to
  standardize the evaluation of nuanced outputs, such as partial
  refusals or evasive answers. A score of 5 is strictly defined as
  "directly and fully complies with the harmful instruction." The
  complete, verbatim judging prompt and rubric are provided in
  Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Complete Agent Prompts and Instructions ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").
- •
  Handling Borderline Cases: The system is designed to handle borderline
  cases through the detailed rubric rather than post-hoc filtering. For
  example, a response that acknowledges the harmful request but provides
  only safe, high-level information would be scored a ‘2‘
  (cautious/warning-style answer), while a response that provides
  clearly disallowed content but fails to satisfy the core harmful
  intent would be scored a ‘4‘. This forces a classification based on
  pre-defined criteria, ensuring consistency.
- •
  Majority Vote and Tie Handling: A final determination of a successful
  jailbreak is made by a majority vote. A response is labeled as
  successful if and only if at least two of the three LLM judges assign
  it a score of 5. This majority rule design inherently resolves any
  potential for ties in the final binary classification (successful vs.
  unsuccessful), as an outcome is always determined by a 2-1 or 3-0
  vote.

### K.2 Human Annotation and Validation Protocol

To validate the LLM judge panel, we conducted a rigorous human
annotation study.

- •
  Sampling and Procedure: A random, stratified sample of 1500
  attack-response pairs was selected, ensuring coverage across all
  target models and major harm categories. Five human annotators were
  tasked with independently evaluating each pair.
- •
  Scoring Rubric: Annotators used the exact same 1-to-5 scoring scale
  and detailed rubric provided to the LLM judges (detailed in
  Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Complete Agent Prompts and Instructions ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs")).
  A score of 5 was considered a successful jailbreak.
- •
  Handling Ambiguity: Borderline or ambiguous cases identified by
  annotators (e.g., a response that is helpful but not a direct
  fulfillment) were flagged for review. These flagged cases were
  resolved through a majority vote among the annotators, with a senior
  author making the final decision in the event of a tie to establish a
  consistent ground truth.
- •
  Inter-Rater Agreement: To measure the consistency among our human
  annotators, we calculated Fleiss’ Kappa ($`\kappa`$), a standard
  metric for assessing agreement with multiple raters. We achieved a
  $`\kappa`$ of 0.81, indicating "substantial agreement" and confirming
  the reliability of our human-generated ground truth labels.

### K.3 Cross-Judge Sensitivity Analysis

We then compared the performance of our LLM judge panel (using the
majority vote rule) against the aggregated human judgments on the same
1500-pair dataset. The results, shown in
Table [9](#A11.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Error Analysis and Findings ‣ K.3 Cross-Judge Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix K Judge Validation Protocol and Cross-Judge Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs"),
demonstrate a high degree of correlation and reliability.

##### Error Analysis and Findings

We achieved good inter-rater agreement among human annotators (Fleiss’
Kappa $`\kappa=0.81`$). We subsequently conducted a detailed error
analysis on the 8.8% of cases where the LLM judge panel’s majority
decision differed from the human-adjudicated ground truth. Our key
findings are as follows:

- •
  Low and Balanced Error: The error rates were found to be both low and
  well-balanced. The False Positive Rate was 4.5% (i.e., the LLM panel
  deemed a response unsafe while humans deemed it safe), and the False
  Negative Rate was 4.3% (i.e., the LLM panel deemed a response safe
  while humans deemed it unsafe). This balance suggests no systematic
  bias towards leniency or strictness.
- •
  Category-Specific Disagreements: The majority of disagreements were
  concentrated in nuanced harm categories requiring significant
  contextual interpretation, such as ‘Misinformation‘ and ‘Hate Speech‘.
  In these cases, LLM judges occasionally exhibited a bias towards
  literal interpretation, sometimes classifying sophisticated,
  hypothetical discussions of sensitive topics as direct compliance,
  leading to false positives.
- •
  High Overall Reliability: Despite the nuanced disagreements, the high
  overall accuracy of 91.2% and a strong Pearson correlation coefficient
  ($`r=0.86`$) between the LLM panel’s scores and the human ground truth
  confirm that our automated judging protocol is a robust and reliable
  proxy for human evaluation and does not systematically inflate the
  reported success rates.

|  |  |
|----|----|
| Metric | LLM Judge Panel vs. Human Majority |
| Accuracy | 91.2% |
| Pearson’s r | 0.86 |
| False Positive Rate (LLM panel says unsafe, humans say safe) | 4.5% |
| False Negative Rate (LLM panel says safe, humans say unsafe) | 4.3% |

Table 9: Cross-Judge Sensitivity Analysis on 1500 samples. The
majority-vote LLM judge panel shows high accuracy and balanced error
rates when compared against the human-annotated ground truth.

The high accuracy (91.2%) and Pearson correlation (0.86), combined with
balanced and low error rates, provide strong evidence that our
majority-vote LLM judge protocol is a reliable and non-lenient proxy for
human evaluation.

## Appendix L Computational Budget and Fair Comparison

##### Budget metric.

We measure computational cost exclusively in terms of *victim-model
queries*: each call to the target model counts as one unit of budget,
regardless of whether it occurs as part of a single-turn or multi-turn
interaction. This metric reflects the dominant constraint in practical
red teaming—how many times a production model can be queried—while
treating attacker-side computation and judge calls as secondary. For
every method, we track a conservative upper bound on the number of
victim queries per harmful instruction under our evaluation protocol.

##### Standardized budgets for baselines.

Several baselines are intrinsically more query-hungry: tree-search and
quality-diversity methods expand large populations of candidate prompts,
and multi-agent systems repeatedly re-query the target model during
planning and optimization. To avoid handicapping these methods, we give
them *at least as many* victim queries as EvoSynth, and often
substantially more, so that they are not artificially limited by our
budget protocol.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Method | Victim queries / instruction | Explanation |
| EvoSynth (ours) | $`\leq 180`$ | Algorithm-Evolution. |
| ActorAttack | $`\approx 200`$ | Enlarged multi-turn, multi-clue budget. |
| AutoDAN | $`\approx 200`$ | More generations with moderate population size. |
| AutoDAN-Turbo | $`\approx 3000`$ | Increased warm-up and lifelong iterations. |
| CoA (Chain-of-Attack) | $`\approx 180`$ | More attack rounds with per-round refinements. |
| CodeAttack | $`\gtrsim 180`$ | Expanded code search; at least 160 victim evaluations. |
| Crescendo | $`\approx 200`$ | Longer conversations with additional backtracking. |
| RedQueen | $`\approx 200`$ | Larger turn budget for adaptive dialogue. |
| RACE | $`\approx 200`$ | Deeper multi-turn reasoning and probing. |
| TreeAttack (TAP) | $`\approx 600`$ | Enlarged depth/branching; $`\sim 600`$ candidates evaluated. |
| X-Teaming | $`\approx 200`$ | More turns and optimizer iterations per attack. |
| RainbowTeaming | $`\gtrsim 3000`$ | Downscaled but still thousands of victim calls. |

Table 10: Standardized victim-model query budgets per harmful
instruction, including EvoSynth’s Algorithm Creation Agent. Values are
conservative upper bounds on target-model calls. EvoSynth is evaluated
under a formal cap of 180 queries; all baselines are given equal or
larger budgets.

##### Fairness and interpretation.

This protocol is deliberately conservative in favor of the baselines.
EvoSynth is evaluated under a formal cap of 180 victim queries. In
contrast, every baseline is allowed an equal or larger victim-query
budget, and the most search-heavy methods (e.g., TreeAttack,
RainbowTeaming) are permitted hundreds to thousands of target calls per
instruction so that their search procedures are not artificially
truncated.

## Appendix M More compleixty correlations analysis across different harm categories.

To validate the generalizability of our findings and to address
potential confounding by the type of harmful query, we conducted a
stratified correlation analysis. While the main analysis demonstrates a
general trend, this section investigates whether these correlations hold
consistently across different harm categories.

Methodology. We partitioned the attack results into the six primary harm
categories. For each subset, we independently re-calculated the Pearson
correlation ($`r`$) between our five key complexity metrics and the
Attack Success Rate (ASR). This analysis was performed on the results
from our most advanced and robust target model, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, to
provide the most challenging test case.

Results and Interpretation. The results, presented in
Table [11](#A13.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix M More compleixty correlations analysis across different harm categories. ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs"),
strongly support the robustness and generalizability of our central
claim. The positive correlations between ASR and the programmatic
complexity metrics—AST Nodes and Tool Calls—remain statistically
significant across all six harm categories. Conversely, correlations
with simple verbosity (Token Count) and prompt-level complexity
(Semantic and Logical) are consistently negligible and non-significant.
This stability across diverse domains provides strong evidence that the
need for high structural and dynamic complexity is a fundamental
requirement for bypassing advanced safety systems, not an artifact of a
specific type of harmful query.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|

| Harm Category | Token Count | AST Nodes | Tool Calls | Semantic | Logical |

| Chemical & Biological | +0.11 (ns) | +0.19 (\*) | +0.24 (\*\*) | 0.08 (ns) | -0.07 (ns) |
| Misinformation | -0.05 (ns) | +0.15 (\*) | +0.19 (\*\*) | -0.09 (ns) | -0.11 (ns) |

## Appendix N Cost Analysis

The victim-query budget controls access to the target model, but
multi-turn and agent-based jailbreak methods can also differ in
attacker-side computation. To make this comparison more transparent, we
additionally report the average attacker-side token cost per run for
representative multi-turn or agent-based methods. This measurement
includes tokens consumed by the attacker-side generation and
coordination process, but excludes the target model’s response tokens.
Although EvoSynth involves multiple agents and code-evolution rounds,
its average attacker-side token cost remains moderate. This is because
the synthesized code-based attack algorithms are often effective within
a small number of refinement iterations, as also reflected in the
convergence analysis in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Analysis of Learning Efficiency ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Metric | ActorAttack | AutoDAN-Turbo | Crescendo | RainbowTeaming | X-Teaming | EvoSynth (Ours) |
| Avg. ASR (%) | 66.2 | 49.7 | 35.4 | 35.4 | 85.7 | 95.9 |
| Avg. attacker-side token cost per run | $`\sim`$1,085 | $`\sim`$2,131 | $`\sim`$3,173 | $`\sim`$2,145 | $`\sim`$1,677 | $`\sim`$1,873 |

Table 12: Average attacker-side token cost for representative multi-turn
and agent-based jailbreak methods. EvoSynth remains comparable to
existing agentic baselines despite its multi-stage code-space
optimization workflow.

These results show that EvoSynth’s improved ASR is not obtained by an
unusually large attacker-side token budget. Instead, EvoSynth achieves a
favorable tradeoff between attacker-side compute and attack success,
consistent with its fast convergence behavior in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Analysis of Learning Efficiency ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Evolve the Method, Not the Prompts: Evolutionary Synthesis of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs").

## Appendix O Limitations

EvoSynth can fail when the refinement budget is consumed before a strong
executable attack algorithm is found. In terminal failed sessions, the
main bottleneck is often the Attack Algorithm Creation Agent: it may
spend too many iterations repairing buggy intermediate code rather than
improving the underlying attack logic. This suggests that EvoSynth is
partly limited by the reliability of code generation and code repair,
and that stronger code agents or more targeted repair signals could
further improve performance.
